title: Healthcare CRM: Buy, Build, or Partner?

Why generic CRMs fail in healthcare and what actually works for medical groups, practices, and digital health companies. RaftLabs 5 min read · Oct 8, 2026 -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Photo by Nappy on Unsplash Most healthcare organizations can’t use a standard CRM. They look at HubSpot or Salesforce, see the price tag, think it’s a fit, and then run into a hard wall: patient data is protected health information, workflows don’t match a sales pipeline, and clinicians won’t switch to a separate system. Three realistic paths exist. One costs $1M+ over three years. Another costs $150K-$330K. The third depends on what your EMR already offers. The problem: Generic CRMs were not built for patient care HIPAA compliance is the obvious first hurdle. Store patient names, contact history, or clinical context in a CRM and that data becomes PHI (Protected Health Information). The vendor needs to sign a Business Associate Agreement. Access controls must be enforced. Audit logs must track who accessed what and when. HubSpot signs BAAs. Salesforce signs BAAs. Smaller CRMs often don’t. But compliance alone isn’t the issue. The deeper problem is that healthcare workflows don’t fit a sales process. A healthcare CRM needs to surface clinical data from the EMR alongside contact history. It needs to track referrals from outside providers and close the loop when a patient is seen. It needs to flag care gaps — patients overdue for screenings, patients who never followed up after a procedure. It needs to coordinate across care team members with role-based visibility into patient data. It needs to handle appointment sequences that don’t look like sales cadences. HubSpot and standard Salesforce don’t have any of this natively. You can build it. But you’re paying a developer to add healthcare logic on top of a sales platform. At that point, you’re already halfway to a custom CRM. Option 1: Salesforce Health Cloud Health Cloud is Salesforce’s purpose-built healthcare platform. It includes care coordination tools, patient timeline views, and pre-built EMR integrations. It’s the market leader. Pricing runs $300–500/user/month depending on the tier. A 50-user deployment costs $180K-$300K/year in licenses alone. Implementation adds $200K-$500K on top for EMR integration, workflow customization, and training. Large health systems often exceed $1M total cost in year one. This works for health systems and large hospital groups with 200+ users, standard care coordination workflows, and IT teams to manage the platform. If you’re running Epic as your EMR, the Epic-Salesforce connector is mature. It breaks down for medical groups, specialty practices, and digital health companies with non-standard patient journeys. Health Cloud is built for a specific care model. If your workflows don’t match it, you spend significant time and money either customizing the platform or compromising your processes. Option 2: EMR-native CRM modules If you already run Epic or Athena as your EMR, their native CRM tools are worth evaluating. Epic’s patient outreach capabilities live inside the system your clinicians already use. No integration lag. No separate login. The trade-off is flexibility. EMR-native tools prioritize clinical workflows, not relationship management. Referral tracking, marketing campaigns, care gap management, and patient retention programs often require workarounds or don’t exist. This fits health systems already deep in Epic who need basic patient outreach without adding another platform. It doesn’t work for complex multi-practice referral networks or organizations needing CRM capabilities beyond what the EMR module supports. Option 3: Custom healthcare CRM A custom-built CRM is purpose-built for your patient workflows, your EMR, and your team’s data model. You own the code. You don’t pay per-seat license fees. Workflows match how your organization actually works. Build cost runs $120K-$250K. Maintenance costs $15K-$40K per year. Timeline is 10–14 weeks from kickoff to production. This suits medical groups and specialty practices that have outgrown their EMR’s tools, telehealth and home health companies with non-standard care models, and organizations processing 10,000+ patient interactions per month where per-seat licensing is painful. What actually gets built in 10–14 weeks: a patient timeline view combining appointments, phone calls, outreach messages, and EMR data pulled via FHIR. A care gap engine that surfaces patients overdue for screenings or follow-ups, automatically flagged in a queue coordinators work through. Referral tracking that logs inbound referrals, assigns them, and tracks outcomes back to the referring provider. Multi-channel outreach via SMS, email, and voice triggered by care gaps or appointment reminders. Role-based access so coordinators see different data than billing staff. Direct integration with Epic, Athena, Cerner, or eClinicalWorks. The math: When custom wins A 50-user Health Cloud deployment costs roughly $650K-$800K in year one (licenses plus implementation). Years two and three cost $180K-$300K annually in licenses and admin. Three-year total: $1M-$1.4M. A 50-user custom CRM costs $120K-$250K to build. Maintenance runs $15K-$40K per year. Three-year total: $150K-$330K. Break-even is typically 24–36 months. If you plan to keep the system for 3+ years, custom wins on cost.
